plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single plot tracing the flight path of a batted ball across a distance-versus-height grid. The horizontal axis is labeled "Distance (ft)" and runs from 0 to 600 with ticks every 100 feet; the vertical axis is labeled "Height (ft)" and carries labeled ticks at 100, 200, and 300, with faint dotted gridlines filling the plotting area. A teal curve leaves the origin, climbs as a broad downward-opening parabola to a maximum slightly above 150 feet near a distance of about 290 feet, then falls back to the horizontal axis a little past 560 feet, with small arrowheads spaced along its length showing the direction of travel. A leader line labeled "Position of hitter" points to the curve's start at the origin, and a second leader labeled "Trajectory of ball" points to a small circular marker on the rising branch near 200 feet. A short red rectangle stands on the horizontal axis at 400 feet and is labeled "Outfield wall"; the curve passes far above its top. Setting the wall directly beneath the arc invites the reader to compare the ball's height at that distance against the height of the barrier. The plot renders a projectile path in a form that settles whether the hit clears the wall.

interactionPlan.concept: Graphing height directly against horizontal distance allows us to evaluate if a projectile clears a physical barrier, independently of how long it took to get there.
elements: x-axis labeled 'Distance (ft)' from 0 to 600 with tick marks every 100 feet
y-axis labeled 'Height (ft)' from 0 to 300 with tick marks every 100 feet
Faint dotted grid lines extending from major tick marks across the plotting area
Teal parabolic curve representing the trajectory, starting at (0,0), peaking around (285, 155), and intersecting the x-axis around (570, 0)
Arrowheads spaced along the teal curve indicating the forward direction of flight
Label 'Position of hitter' with a leader line pointing to the origin (0,0)
Label 'Trajectory of ball' with a leader line pointing to the curve
Interactive baseball marker that slides along the trajectory curve
Vertical drop line (dashed) connecting the baseball marker to the x-axis, displaying current height and distance
Red rectangle resting on the x-axis representing the 'Outfield wall'
Label 'Outfield wall' floating just above the red rectangle

interactions.label: Ball distance from hitter
interactions.teaches: The curve dictates exactly how high the ball is at any given horizontal distance from home plate.

interactions.label: Outfield wall position
interactions.teaches: Clearing the wall is a direct comparison of two heights at a single specific x-value: the trajectory's height y(x) versus the wall's height.

interactions.label: Display mode
interactions.teaches: The continuous flight path is composed of an infinite set of discrete (distance, height) coordinate solutions.

demo_steps.title: Tracing the flight path
demo_steps.narration: The graph models height as a function of horizontal distance. Drag the ball to see its height rise and fall as it moves further from the hitter.

demo_steps.title: Clearing the fence
demo_steps.narration: Move the ball to 400 feet, exactly where the wall is positioned. The ball's height on the curve is much higher than the top of the wall, so it clears easily.

demo_steps.title: Moving the wall back
demo_steps.narration: If the wall were pushed back to 530 feet, try moving the ball there. At this distance, the trajectory has dropped so low that the ball would hit the wall.

demo_steps.title: A sequence of coordinates
demo_steps.narration: Toggling to sampled points reveals that this smooth path is just a series of mapped (x, y) coordinates generated by projectile equations.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Plotting a projectile's path as y versus x removes time from the picture, turning a dynamic physics problem into a simple geometric comparison of heights.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Ensure the axes are strictly bounded (x: 0-600, y: 0-300). The trajectory should be a smooth downward-opening parabola originating at (0,0), reaching a maximum y of ~155 near x=285, and returning to y=0 near x=570. The outfield wall is a distinct, short red rectangle on the x-axis whose horizontal position responds to the slider. When 'Sampled points' is active, fade out the solid teal line and display prominent teal dots along the same path instead.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for distance from the hitter: the learner drags a marker along the trajectory, the height readout and vertical drop to the x-axis update, and the parabola's height-at-distance relationship becomes concrete.
- Slider for outfield wall position: the learner moves the wall left or right, the figure highlights whether the ball is above or below the wall at that distance, and clearing the wall becomes a comparison of two heights at one x-value.
- Toggle between path and sampled points: the learner switches from the smooth trajectory to discrete distance-height samples, the same arc appears as points on the grid, and the connection between graph, table values, and projectile motion becomes clear.

authoredContext:
The ball is 141.8 feet in the air when it soars out of the ballpark. It was indeed a home run. See the figure.

Plotted trajectory of a hit ball, showing the position of the batter at the origin, the ball's path in the shape of a wide downward facing parabola, and the outfield wall as a vertical line segment rising to 10 ft under the ball's path.
